set.hook: The Disfrutar chefs' first restaurant: a shared tasting menu in a stone house on the Riera de Sant Vicenç.
set.why: Mateu Casañas, Oriol Castro and Eduard Xatruch opened this room in 2012, after elBulli closed and before they started Disfrutar in Barcelona. Disfrutar went on to win its third MICHELIN star in November 2023 and to top the World's 50 Best list in June 2024. Here the idea is older and simpler: every plate goes to the middle of the table. The fixed chef's menu runs to about ten savoury courses and three desserts, served in a slate-and-stone house on the dry riverbed.

set.hook: Market tapas and flamed oysters on a water's-edge terrace looking back across the harbour at the white town.
set.why: Talla sits on Riba Pitxot, the west side of the bay, so its terrace faces the church and the white houses rather than the open sea; Frommers calls it perhaps the best-placed table in Cadaqués. Time Out says it began as a cultural bar started by the Catalan actor and musician Bruno Oro, and turned into a restaurant after neighbours complained about the noise. The kitchen now works from the market: oysters finished over flame, tartares, rice.

set.hook: The Seriñana family's fish house in the old sea wall since 1967, now run by the third generation.
set.why: Quimet Seriñana and Maria Torrents opened it in 1967 inside the bastion that once guarded the town from pirates. Today Adrià Seriñana cooks and his sister Aina runs the wine. In an August 2026 interview with Ara she explained two habits: she adds only about 13 or 14 euros to a bottle over its shop price, and the list prints the distance in kilometres from the restaurant to each winery, so foreign guests can see how close the Empordà vines are.

set.hook: No menu card, shared tables: the Mota family's kitchen since 1960, where the day's dishes are recited aloud.
set.why: Ana Mota learned to cook from Cadaqués neighbours she worked for as a babysitter, then opened her own room in 1960; success later let the family buy a house a little further down the street, where Casa Anita still stands. She died in June 2025, three days short of her ninetieth birthday, and Ara gave her an obituary. Her son Juanito and daughter Ana Mari now cook. Ara's best story: Kirk Douglas once settled an unpaid bill with a thick stack of banknotes.

set.hook: A seafront fish-and-rice house opened in 1982 by the family that now also makes Cap de Creus wine.
set.why: Rafa Martín Mota, son of Casa Anita's founder, opened Can Rafa on the Passeig in 1982 with his wife Carmen Faixó, who still makes the desserts. In 2000 the family planted vines on the cape and built Celler Martín Faixó, a winery with a guesthouse at Mas Perafita, so the bottles on the table come from a few kilometres away. Ara reported in October 2025 that, after some twenty years of permit battles, work on a new underground cellar was due to start in 2026.

set.hook: A small family kitchen one lane back from the water, cooking scorpionfish, suquet and urchins in season.
set.why: La Sirena works from a narrow lane, Carrer des Call, a block up from the front, in a room decorated with mermaids. It is a family house that cooks the local catch the old way: scorpionfish with its sauce and potatoes, suquet and zarzuela fish stews, paella. In the cold months it serves garoines, the sea urchins Cadaqués eats from January to March, which makes it one of the few tables here worth seeking out in winter.

set.hook: Paella, fideuà and fish from a charcoal oven, on the Passeig facing the beach.
set.why: S'Estrop takes its name from the rope loop that holds an oar to a fishing boat's thole pin, and it sits on the Plaça del Passeig with tables looking across the beach. A set lunch lets you take a rice or fideuà as the main course, which makes it one of the cheaper ways to eat rice on the front.

set.hook: Curries by the lighthouse at mainland Spain's easternmost point, served since 1991 in an old Civil Guard post.
set.why: In 1991 Christopher Little, a British chef, took over the former Guardia Civil barracks beside the Cap de Creus lighthouse and turned it into a restaurant. He still runs it, and the menu reflects him: samosas, chutneys, seven curries (meat, fish or vegetable) and a vindaloo, alongside Catalan seafood. The terrace looks over Cala Culip and the open sea; in winter the tramuntana wind can make lunch a battle.

set.hook: The beach bar on the sand since 1935: breakfast, tapas and a flaming cremat at dusk.
set.why: The Marítim opened on Sant Jaume's day, 25 July 1935, and turned ninety in 2025, which makes it one of the oldest bars on the bay. In 2018 the Alt Empordà county council listed it as a Bé Cultural d'Interès Local, a protected local heritage site. Dalí, Duchamp and García Márquez are among the patrons the press names, and Dalí is said to have arrived by boat. Today it serves breakfasts by the water, tapas and the fishermen's cremat.

set.hook: The seafront bar whose logo Dalí drew in 1975, now a restaurant with a terrace and memorabilia walls.
set.why: L'Hostal was founded by an Italian, Marci Pogany, and accounts call it the only bar Dalí frequented in Cadaqués; out of friendship he drew and signed its logo for free, dated 1975 by two listings. In the 1960s and 70s it was a late-night club where Mick Jagger, Keith Richards and García Márquez turned up. The club has gone: today it is a seafront restaurant with a terrace, the walls still covered in Dalí material.
